EARL D. BABST, IOTA-PHI '93
PSI
UPSILON has been con
spicuously fortunate in the dis
tinguished men who have been priv
ileged to direct the destinies of
our Fraternity. As President of the
Executive Council from 1924 to
1929, Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93,
held the highest ofl&ce of trust and
honor which Psi Upsilon can be
stow. One of the country's leading
citizens, he was the sixth President
of the Council, which was insti
tuted in 1869, being preceded by
WUliam F. Morgan, Delta '65,
Frederic A. Brown, Lambda '72,
Thomas Thacher, Beta '71, Ward
McLean, Theta '43, and Herbert L.
Bridgman, Gamma '66. His was in
deed a difficult task. While the
Fraternity was still recovering from
the shock of the sudden death of
Herbert L. Bridgman on Septem
ber 24, 1924, Brother Babst was
elected to succeed the person who
for forty-one years had been our
dearly beloved President, a verita
ble "Ark of the Covenant," as he
was affectionately called. His elec
tion proved to be a surprise to him.
In writing to one of his associates on
the Council, Brother Babst said:
"I find myself somewhat under the
spell of the honor and responsibility
I assumed Tuesday evening! No one
had spoken to me in advance.
Naturally, I will do all I can to
meet your expectations and trust,
but shall lean heavily on you and
the others."
Born in Crestline, Ohio, July 6,
1870, the son of Jacob Babst and
Mathilda Stoll Babst, he attended
the Kenyon Military Academy, and
entered Kenyon College in 1889.
It was there that he joined the Iota
Chapter and became a member of
the Fraternity which he has long
served with distinction and devo
tion. In his many graceful and
beautiful addresses at Psi Upsilon
functions, he has always referred to
the "Dear Old Spot" of the Iota
with loving tenderness. At our Cen
tennial at the Theta he said that he
"would not abandon his recollection
of the 'Dear Old Spot' of the Iota
for any of the chapter houses of the
present day." In 1891 Brother Babst
transferred to the University of
Michigan and became a distin
guished member of the Phi Chapter.
His interest in the Fraternity at
large began at an early date. He was
a delegate of the Phi to the Conven
tion at the Zeta in 1893, and was a
bearer of the Wisconsin petition
for the Rho Chapter. He received
the degree of Bachelor of Philosophy
in 1893 and the LL.B. degree a year
later. For his scholastic attain
ments he was elected to Phi Beta
Kappa. In 1911 the University of
Michigan conferred an honorary
Master of Arts upon him, and in
1926 Kenyon College bestowed an
LL.D. degree.
In 1903 Brother Babst married
Alice Edwina Uhl, the daughter of
the late Edwin F. Uhl, one time
Assistant Secretary of State and
Ambassador to Germany. Admitted
to the Michigan Bar in 1894, for
eight years he was associated with
the Hon. Otto Kirchner in practice
in Detroit. During this period he
was a founder of the Detroit Uni-
Earl D. Babst, lota-Phi '93, for five years President of the Executive Council

versify School and of the Detroit
University Club, also a director of
the Citizens Savings Bank. From
1902 to 1906 Brother Babst was a
member of the firm of Green,
Peters and Babst in Chicago, serv
ing as general counsel of the
National Biscuit Company, of the
American Radiator Company, and
others. In 1906 he moved to New
York as general counsel and later
as first Vice-President of the
National Biscuit Company. In 1915
he was elected President of the
American Sugar Refining Company,
which office he held until 1925.
During the War, as a member of the
International Sugar Commission, he
represented the United States in
the allocation of sugar supplies to
the Allies. Since 1925 he has been
the chairman of the board of the
American Sugar Refining Company.
He is also a director of the Chase
National Bank and of many com
panies.
In spite of his busy career Brother
Babst has always found time to
render service to Kenyon and to
Michigan. From 1926 to 1937 he
was a trustee of Kenyon College and
Alumni Council. He served on the
Executive Committee of the Alumni
Advisory Council of the University
of Michigan from 1907 to 1923.
He was President of the University
of Michigan Club of New York,
1912-1913; President of the Kenyon
Alumni Association of the East,
1915-1917, 1923-1926.
Through his long and distin
guished career Brother Babst has al
ways been a loyal supporter of Psi
Upsilon. His invaluable book, "Oc
casions in Psi Upsilon," containing
his addresses at fraternity affairs.
is filled with his devotion to Psi
Upsilon, which to him "has ever
been a fascinating romance," while
"at the same time in its brotherhood
it has been a living reality." His
interest in the activities of the Fra
ternity has ever "been a labor of
love, a happy labor." His service on
the Council from 1907 to 1929 is but
typical of the willingness of the
prominent and busy leaders in our
nation's life to accept long tenures
of Council service. Brother Herbert
L. Bridgman's forty-seven years of
continuous service on the Council is
without parallel in the history of
college fraternities. Brother Ben
jamin H. Bayliss, Delta '65, served
for fourteen years. Brother Herbert
S. Houston, Omega '88, for fifteen
years. Brother Francis S. Bangs,
Lambda '78, for seventeen years.
Brother William M. Kingsley, Delta
'83, for seventeen years. Brother
George Henry Fox, Upsilon '67, for
twenty years. Brother Edward L.
Stevens, Chi '99, for twenty-two
years. Brother George S. Coleman,
Xi '76, for twenty-three years.
Brothers R. Bourke Corcoran,
Omega '15, and Emmett Hay Nay
lor, Zeta '09, have been members of
the Council since 1920 and 1919
respectively.
We are proud that Brother Babst
is a Psi U, we are proud of his leader
ship, his lofty ideals and his noble
purposes. His keen judgment, his
generous understanding of the grad
uate and the undergraduate alike,
his lovable character, have made
him one of our greatest leaders. He
epitomized the spirit of Psi Upsilon
when he said: "The badge flashes
many ideals�
honor, integrity, cour
tesy and chivalry."

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL TESTIMONIAL
DINNER TO ARCHIBALD DOUGLAS,
LAMBDA '94
THE
PRESENT and former
members of the Executive Coun
cil tendered a testimonial dinner to
Brother Douglas on November 22nd
at the Union League Club of New
York City. Knowing "Archie"
Douglas' desire for simplicity it was
decided to limit the invitations to
the dinner to the Presidents of the
Alumni Association of each Chap
ter, the Board of Governors of the
Alumni Association of Psi Upsilon,
a group of very active Alumni of his
own Chapter, the Lambda, and a
very few close friends of his in the
Fraternity.
In order to meet with our guest's
crowded list of engagements, the
dinner was called on rather short
notice, but about 35 brothers from
16 chapters gathered about the great
round festive board. Telegrams and
letters came from nearly every ac
tive chapter and many fine letters
arrived from those invited but who
could not attend.
It all was a fine tribute to the high
esteem in which "Archie" Douglas
is held by Psi Upsilon. In order to
keep such a gathering from being
an ordeal for our guest of honor, it
was decided to have no formal ad
dresses and thus with a desired air
of informality and much fine singing
the evening was a delight to all
present. Walter T. Collins, Iota '03,
and Eugene S. Wilson, Gamma '02,
led the singing. Brother Werrenrath
being on a concert tour.
In the absence of President Scott
Turner, Phi '02, R. Bourke Cor
coran, Omega '15, a Vice President
of the Council, presided.
The Union League Club of New
York outdid itself in the dinner ar
rangements. For many years the
Council meetings have been held
there and in view of the fact that
Archibald Douglas is one of the
Club's older members (being 158th
among 1800) the famous gold
service of the Club was used. The
American, Canadian and Psi U flags
reposed in their standards. Follow
ing dinner each brother present was
introduced and then the former
members of the Council present were
presented in a group followed by a
like introduction of the present
Council members. Next was a toast
to the President of the United States
and the King of England. The next
item was a toast to the seven
Founders of Psi Upsilon, and then
a toast to Herbert L. Bridgman,
Gamma '66, for 41 years President
of Psi U, and Dr. George Henry
Fox, Upsilon '67, late Honorary
President of the Executive Council.
After reading the large accumula
tion of letters and telegrams the
Chairman asked Brother Cadwalla
der Evans, Eta '01, a new member of
the Council, to give a brief oral re
port of his recent trip to the West
Coast which included an official
visit to the three West Coast Chap
ters, the Epsilon, Theta Theta and
Zeta Zeta.
Herbert Houston, Omega '88,

tribute to Brother Douglas, whom
he described as a great lawyer

Brother Houston continued : "The
Diamond, as it comes from the press

faith of the Committee and the
Council who joined in reestablishing
it, by being a real means of com
munication between every member
of the Fraternity and all the other
members of the Fraternity. At the
University of Washington where I
stopped on my way back from
Japan, the members of the chapter
told me that The Diamond kept
them informed on what was going on
in the Fraternity as a whole and I
am sure that every member of
every chapter feels that way about
the magazine. Some day we must
realize Brother Babst's dream of
having the Bridgman endowment
fund for The Diamond large enough
to insure the magazine going to
every member of the Fraternity in
every part of the world."
In closing his address. Brother
Houston said that he had been de
lighted to hear from Brother Albert
C. Jacobs of The Diamond that the
magazine was going to carry several
pages of Brother William Howard
Taft's address at the dinner given
in his honor in Washington in 1929.
Brother Houston said he would like
to suggest that the entire address be
put in a very attractive printed
form and that the Executive Council
propose to every chapter that it be
made part of the ritual to read it
at the first chapter meeting at the
beginning of every college year.
Brother Houston gave it as his
opinion that "in no other way can a
more vivid interpretation be given
of the importance of scholarship to
the individual Psi U than in the
searching challenge which Brother
Taft presented in that address."
John Godfrey Saxe, Lambda '00
(McGiU '97), spoke for the Lambda
Chapter and as a former member of
the Council. Coming from a family
of distinguished Psi U's and business
achievement, and himself an out
standing member of the New York
Bar, he voiced the pride of Colum
bia and the Lambda because Archie
Douglas had done so much for
them. He recalled the many mem
bers of Archie's family in Psi U, and
in his usual eloquence brought the
gathering to a high pitch in a rousing
tribute to our guest.
The toastmaster requested Broth
er Edward L. Stevens, Chi '99, to
give the official greetings and trib
ute of the Fraternity to Brother
Douglas. Ned Stevens for twentytwo years was a member of the
Council and its President for five
years through our great Centennial
in 1933.
With his noted personal charm

72 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON
and warm heart Ned Stevens out
lined the achievements of Psi Upsi
lon while our guest was a member
of the Council and its distinguished
President. He said :
"Psi Upsilon's alumni have to
night paid their tribute to our
honored guest, a tribute sincere and
well deserved. What I should like to
add is from what I believe to be the
viewpoint of our undergraduates;
for I know that the boys of our old
Fraternity love Archie Douglas.
"For many years, each succeed
ing college generation at his own
Chapter has learned through per
sonal experience his untiring inter
est in them and their problems.
His brotherly advice has ever been
at their service, when requested, and
his quiet generosity has made their
Chapter House a real Home. Above
all, his example, as the man whom
Columbia University has oflScially
designated 'the ideal Alumnus,' has
been a continuing inspiration to his
younger brothers at West 115th
Street. And now, during three and a
half of the four years which have
followed our great Centennial, he
has shown our other Chapters as
well, our active Psi U's especially,
that same interest in their welfare
and helpful understanding of their
needs and aspirations which the
Lambda Chapter has known so
long.
"It was my good fortune to be
present at the installation of our
newest Chapter at Vancouver, two
years ago last month, when Brother
Harry Logan, of the Epsilon Phi
Chapter and the Faculty of the
University of British Columbia,
read aloud to that great gathering
of old and very new Psi U's a mes
sage from Archie Douglas as Presi
dent of the Executive Council,
which The Diamond for Novem
ber, 1935, has preserved for us.
There was a moment of silence,
then tremendous applause, as the
man who had been only a name to
those new Brothers became a real
and living personality. Then Doctor
Walter Sage, of the Zeta Zeta and
the University of British Columbia
Faculty, whispered to me, 'Beauti
ful thoughts and wonderfully ex
pressed;' and I answered, 'Archie
Douglas is not only a capable busi
ness man and a great lawyer, but,
as you know now and I've long
realized, a poet as well.' My thoughts
went back to what Archie had once
told me of that walking-trip through
the British Isles which he and that
other Lambda poet. Brother Guy
Wetmore Carryl, had taken more
than forty years before, with shrines
dear to poets the world over as their
objectives, particularly the home of
Robert Louis Stevenson.
"
'Beautiful thoughts, wonderfully
expressed!' Psi Upsilon's early days
linked up with the present and I
thought of another ardent Psi U
of more than a century before,
young Merwin Stewart, whose own
beautiful thoughts found wonderful
expression in the Preamble to our
Fraternity's Constitution and the
Initiation Ritual, into which he
poured his poetic and prophetic Psi
U loyalty during that long-ago
Christmas vacation of 1833; and
which have come down to us, prac
tically unchanged, to thrill us anew
whenever we read them or hear
them spoken. For he, just as Archie
Douglas, understood the inarticu
late yearnings of college boys for the

THEDIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON 73
friendship and companionship of
young men of kindred tastes and
ideals, between whom an inter
change of the most intimate and
sacred feelings of the heart might be
possible; he, too, had the ability and
the inspiration to give those yearn
ings worthy expression.
"Too often, these fine aspirations
of our younger brothers have been
disappointed; too often, we older
Psi U's have failed to understand
their needs and their hopes, for there
is a gap bfetween age and youth that
only deep wisdom and insight can
bridge. And so I count it chief,
among the many worth-while serv
ices which Archie Douglas has laid
upon our common altar, that he has
read aright these unspoken yearn
ings of our fine young men and has
brought to them the bright hope
of fulfilment."
The response of Brother Douglas
was as beautiful and sincere as
everyone who is privileged to know
him, knew it would be. He was
visibly affected by the tributes paid
to him. In his usual modesty he dis
claimed any earned credit for the
many honors paid him but he
strongly attested his firm belief in
the one hundred and four years of
tradition of Psi Upsilon�
its beauti
ful emphasis on fine friendships
�
its outstanding services over many
decades to the colleges and uni
versities where we have chapters;
the public and personal services of
our thousands of alumni great and
small to their respective interests,
and saying in closing that next to
his family life, Psi Upsilon was the
most touching and lasting experi
ence of his life.
There followed many brief talks
by others present. The dinner
closed after singing "Dear Old
Shrine," and "Brothers, the Day is
Ended."
Afterwards many of the brothers
remained for further reunions�
story telling and much fine sing
ing.

EUGENE SMITH VS^ILSON, GAMMA 02
By Frederick S. Fales, Gamma '96
EUGENE
SMITH WILSON, Gamma '02, died of a heart attack after
a short illness on Sunday, December 19th, at his home, 35 East 76th
Street, New York City. He was 58 years old.
Brother Wilson was born in Bloomfield, N. J., on
May 30th, 1879, a son
of Robert Patterson Wilson and Mary Jennette Smith Wilson. He was
graduated from Adelphi Academy, in Brooklyn, in 1898, and from Amherst
College in 1902. He served as Captain of the track team at Amherst during
his senior year. He studied law at Washington University, receiving his
LL.B. degree in 1904.
During the next ten years Brother Wilson practiced law in St. Louis,
being retained as general counsel for Wisconsin, Cleveland, Michigan and
Chicago telephone companies, and in 1914 he entered the employment of
the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, and was a Vice-Presi
dent of that company at the time of his death. During the last five years he
has served as their special counsel in Washington.
Following the death from infantile paralysis of the youngest of his three
sons. Brother Wilson devoted considerable time campaigning against the
disease, and became a trustee of the Georgia Warm Springs Foundation.
He was also a trustee of Deerfield Academy, Deerfield, Mass.
Since 1930 he has been a member of the Executive Council of the Fra
ternity, and for over three years of that period acted as its Vice-President.
He was also President of the Corporation of the Gamma Chapter.
Surviving are his wife, the former Margaret Grey Whitelaw, of St. Louis,
whom he married in 1904; two sons, Eugene S. Wilson, Jr., of Morristown,
N. J., and Robert W. Wilson, of Alexandria, Va., both members of the
Gamma Chapter, and a sister, Mrs. A. Stewart White, of White Plains.
The following Resolution has been adopted by the Executive Council:
It is with a feeling of deep sorrow that we, the members of the Executive Council of
Psi Upsilon, record the death on December nineteenth, nineteen hundred and
thirty-seven, of our fellow member, Eugene Smith Wilson, Gamma 1902.
Brother Wilson served on the Executive Council continuously since the Convention
of 1930, and for over three years of that period acted as its Vice-President. He gave
generously both of his time and of his energies to the fraternity. Loyal and devoted
in service, wise in experience, sound and fair in judgment, cheerful and courageous
in spirit, kindly and considerate in word and act, he leaves a place in our ranks
which it will indeed be difficult to fill.
But even keener than our appreciation of his services is our sense of great personal
loss. His remarkable personality, his spirit of enthusiasm rare beyond the years of
youth, his keen but kindly sense of humor, his dependability and his manlinessmany were the traits which made us respect and love him as a friend.
To his wife and to his family we ofiFer our deepest sympathy and express our sincere
hope that they may find comfort in their sorrow.

convention of the Protestant Epis
copal Church. Shortly thereafter
Brother William Lee Richards,
Theta '22, General Secretary, Field
Department, of the National Coun
cil of the Protestant Episcopal
Church, sent the Editor of The
Diamond the excellent picture of
the members of our Fraternity at
the Convention. A request was at
once made of Brother Richards to
tell how the picture came to be
taken. The Diamond takes pleasure
in publishing his interesting reply.
"Dear Brother Jacobs:
"Your have asked me to tell you
something about how a picture
came to be taken of Psi U's at
general Convention in Cincinnati.
To me, it is an inspiring memory.
"My work takes me out of town
a great deal and I am constantly on
the lookout for diamond shaped
badges. I have met many Dekes,
Phi Gams and S.A.E.'s, but my luck
seems to run out in locating Psi U's.
By the time I arrived in Cincinnati
on October 2nd I had completely
lost hope. In fact, I was in a frame
of mind where meeting one Psi U
would have seemed like running into
my old room mate.
"Just then I met Bishop Roberts
of South Dakota (Beta Beta '05).
Seeing a diamond on his vest, I re
marked that I wished his badge had
the right letters as well as the right
"
'What should they be?', he

"
'Psi U,' said I, being equal to
any occasion.
"That started it. The Bishop
knew one or two Psi U's and each
of them knew one or two and so it
went. Messages were sent to every
part of the city and to all depart
ments of the convention to the
effect that the Psi U's were going to
gather. The interest was amazing to
everyone but a Psi U.
"When a suitable day and hour
were decided upon, announcements

Henry Power Field, Gamma '80

Judge Henry Power Field of the Pro
bate Court of Hampshire County, Mass.,
died of heart disease in Northampton on
September 30, 1937, at the age of sev
enty-eight. Born in New London, Conn.,
October 29, 1858, a descendant of
Zachariah Field who settled in Dorches
ter, Mass., in 1630, graduating from
Amherst in 1880, Judge Field received
the LL.B. degree from the University of
Michigan two years later. Admitted to
the Massachusetts Bar in 1883, he prac
ticed his chosen profession in Northamp
ton until 1919, at which time he was
appointed special judge of the Probate
Court of Northampton. In 1923 he ac
cepted an appointment as Judge of the
Probate Court for Hampshire County
which position he held until his death.
He twice declined an appointment to the
Superior Court of Massachusetts. His
alma mater recognized his distinguished
service by conferring an honorary LL.D.
degree upon him.
In 1895 Judge Field sponsored Calvin
Coolidge for admission to the Hampshire
County Bar and it was in his office that
the late President of the United States
began his legal career. After the Presi
dential Election in 1920, Judge Field,
as a Presidential elector, nominated
Calvin Coolidge for Vice-President of
the United States in the formal cere
monies held by the Massachusetts mem
bers of the Electoral College.
Mayor of Northampton in 1896, a
member of the Massachusetts Board of
Insanity, a former President of the
Amherst Alumni Association, a Trustee
of the Forbes Library in Northampton
and of the State Hospital for the Insane,
Judge Field was from 1907 to 1915 the
chairman of the Executive Committee
of the Massachusetts Republican Com
mittee.
His father was a graduate of Amherst
in the class of 1834 and was a member of
the Faculty of Amherst College for four
teen years. "With this background,"
reads the resolution adopted by the
Gamma Chapter at its recent initiation,
"it is easy to understand his great love
for Amherst and his deep interest in
everything pertaining to the welfare of
the college.
"He once said at one of our banquets
that the one and only influence that
caused him to return to Massachusetts
to practice law was 'the magnetic spell
of Amherst.'
"The same magnetic spell continued
to draw him back to Amherst and to
Psi Upsilon each succeeding year for
Commencement and for our initiation
ceremonies and for many other occa
sions. . . .
"And now let the records of the
Gamma Chapter ... be opened that we
may fittingly inscribe therein our great
loss in the death of Brother Henry
Power Field, our pride in his fellowship
and our
appreciation of a life well lived."
The members of the Gamma Chapter
residing in St. Louis, Mo., adopted a
resolution fittingly expressing their deep
sorrow and regret over the death of
Brother Field.

sistant and associate in American history

was professor of history at Brown. Then
followed four years as head of the his
tory department of the University of
Chicago. From 1905 to 1928 he was di
rector of the Department of Historical
Research of the Carnegie Institution of
Washington. Managing editor of the
American Historical Review from 1895

sions, 1895 to 1899, and again, 1905 to
1908, he was president of the American
Historical Association from 1906 to 1907.

Henry Clay Folger, the Standard Oil
magnate. Dr. Jameson was largely re
sponsible for the building of the Folger
Shakespeare Library in Washington.
When Mr. Folger first began to plan to
dispose of his great collection of Eliza
bethan books and manuscripts, Dr.
Jameson suggested that they be given

dedicated April 23, 1932.

Lansing Parmelee Reed, Beta '04
(A Distinguished Corporation Lawyer)
Lansing Parmelee Reed, a corporation
lawyer in the firm of Davis, Polk, Wardwell, Gardiner and Reed, died December
2, 1937 of double pneumonia at his
home in New York City. Fifty-five
years of age, he was the youngest of the
partners which gave the legal firm its
name.
Born in New York City, the son of a
Congregational minister. Brother Reed
graduated from Phillips Academy, An
dover, Mass., of which he was later
a trustee, and from Yale College where
he was a member of Phi Beta Kappa and
of SkuU and Bones. He received his legal
training at the Harvard Law School
where he was an editor of the Harvard
Law Review.
In 1931, the magazine Fortune listed
Mr. Reed among the nine leading busi
ness lawyers in the city, saying, "His
reputation, in spite of his years, is of the
old-fashioned sort. His judgment is
valued, not merely because it takes the
form of an expertly drawn and bril
liantly conceived legal opinion, but be
cause it is his judgment. And his integ
rity is a positive attribute and one that
is noticed even among men whose integ
rity is never questioned. His candor and
sense of professional honor have con
tributed to his success. He has actually
profited from them."
Mr. Reed was a director of the Inter
national Telephone and Telegraph Cor
poration and Standard Brands, Inc.,
and a former director of the Guaranty
Trust Company of New York, as well as
one of the principal legal representatives
of these firms. He was Vice-President
of the Board of Trustees of the Union
Theological Seminary and a trustee
of the Madison Avenue Presbyterian
Church and a director of the Young
Men's Christian Association of New
York. He was also a trustee of the New
York Public Library and of Miss
Chapin's School.
Surviving are his mother, his wife,
Mrs. Ruth Lawrence Reed, daughter of
Bishop WiUiam Lawrence, of Massa
chusetts, retired, a brother, Edward B.
Reed, Beta '94, a sister, and five
daughters.
